SM18L-A1.free_elimination: -12 is a sign-flipped echo of the printed 12 (the 'forgot to scale' distractor). No sign kill: all four options negative and c must be negative.
SM18L-A1.note: Printed numbers: 4,6 (coefficients), 9,6 (coefficients), 12 (constant). Ratio 2/3 links every pair; c = 12*(2/3) with sign, so a student who 'scales the constant by the coefficient ratio' lands on the key by pattern. Wrong-method coincidence: 12-4 = 8 (constant minus coefficient), sign-flipped. Routine substitution y=(6x+12)/9 into eq1 collapses to -8 = c with no parallel-slope insight at all, so the 'at least one solution' twist is bypassed by ordinary procedure.

SM18L-A2.free_elimination: 48 = 21+27 (sum of the two printed constants) and also exceeds 27, the x-cap that y>=0 with y<=-x+27 imposes on sight. 7 and 15 need the vertex.
SM18L-A2.note: Printed: 3 (slope), 21 (intercept), 1 (slope), 27 (intercept), 0,0. Vertices (0,0),(7,0),(12,15),(0,27) - the region IS a quadrilateral as claimed. Options are exactly {x-intercept, x-vertex, y-vertex, sum of intercepts}; distractor 7 is a vertex x so a student who lists vertices sees 7 and 12 both and must pick the larger, which is the only decision. Nothing beyond routine intersection; real SAT hard route would ask for a max of a linear objective, not a coordinate.

SM18L-A3.free_elimination: 12 = 4*3, a product of two printed numbers (the input step without the slope). Near-free: the answer is slope*12 and slope = 15/5 is integer, so the key must be a multiple of 12 - kills 41 and 45 as well, leaving 12 vs 36 and 12 already struck.
SM18L-A3.note: Printed: 2,11,7,26 (table), 4,1 (inside g), 3 (shift). Roles tested: 11 and 26 are outputs; 41 = 36+5 uses the intercept 5, which is irrelevant to a difference - a student who knows differences kill intercepts strikes it. Routine route f(x)=3x+5, g(t)=12t+2, difference 36 needs no insight. Wrong-method coincidence: 4*(2+7)=36. Divisibility-by-12 is cheaper than solving and leaves one live distractor, so this is closer to n_struck=3 for an alert student.

SM18L-A4.free_elimination: None strictly free. 12 = 2*6 (doubled printed number, the forgot-to-divide answer) and 21 = 3*5+6 are printed-number closures but each is a plausible error, not a structural kill.
SM18L-A4.note: Printed: 3 (coefficient), 6 (bound), 5 (midpoint). The midpoint 5 does NOTHING for the asked quantity - the length is 2*6/3 regardless of c. That is the intended insight, but the routine path (c = 15, endpoints 3 and 7, length 4) is two lines and reaches the key, so the decoy costs nothing. Wrong-method coincidence: 7-3 = 4 also equals endpoint-minus-endpoint, which IS the method; 6-... no other. A student who reads |3x-c|<=6 as 'x within 2 of c/3' answers on sight. Medium at best on the real hard route.

SM18L-A5.free_elimination: 148 = 180-32, difference of two printed constants; and it is struck by range on sight - the least possible cost is a 10-page job, which must cost LESS than the printed 50-page $32, so the difference must exceed 148.
SM18L-A5.note: Printed: 50,32,100,52 (two data points), 10 (min pages), 180 (cost cap). All four options are 180 minus something, so the item reduces to 'what is the min cost': 32 (148), 12 = setup (168), 4 = 10 pages of paper (176), 16 (164). The cap being in dollars while the floor is in pages is the only decision point and it is a reading step, not a math one. Max cost is exactly 180 because 420 pages is an integer job - representation fine. No wrong-method coincidence found for 164.

SM18L-A6.free_elimination: None free. All options exceed 5 and k>5 is forced (coefficient -8/(k-5) = -4), so no sign kill available.
SM18L-A6.note: Printed: k, 2 (y-coef), 5 (x-coef), 3 (k-coef), 6 (y-coef), -4 (target y-coef). WRONG-METHOD COINCIDENCE: 5+2 = 7 - the two most visible coefficients sum to the key; also 13-6 = 7. A student who guesses 'k equals the other x-coefficient plus the y-coefficient' is rewarded. Routine solve-for-x reaches the key with no insight; c = 21/2 is never needed. 21 = 3*7 is a closure over the key, harmless. Medium.

SM18L-A7.free_elimination: 4 is struck by reading alone: it zeroes the printed denominator (x-4). That is the extraneous root offered as an option, so the item's whole decision point is a free kill for anyone who scans the denominators.
SM18L-A7.note: Printed: 3,4 (numerator/denominator), 4,2, 42. Cleared: x^2+9x-52 = (x+13)(x-4). Discriminant 81+208 = 289 = 17^2, consistent. Roots -13 and 4, both offered - good: the unchecked solver must still choose. But the SAT places rational equations in Advanced Math (nonlinear equations in one variable), not Algebra, so this is off the Algebra blueprint. Plug-in bypass is heavy (10/17 - 4/11 = 42/187) so the insight is not routinely bypassable. -5 and 11 are algebra-slip answers. Wrong-method coincidence: 3-16 = -13 is not a natural route. Only genuinely hard item so far, in the wrong domain.

SM18L-B1.free_elimination: 126 = 186-60: the key and one distractor differ by exactly the printed fixed fee, so the pair is visible and the fee-less one falls. 74 and 102 sit on the same 60+0.35*(40*3^k) ladder (k=0,1,2) so the ladder itself tells the student which is 'fully converted'.
SM18L-B1.note: Printed: 60 (fee), 0.35 (rate), 40 (area, sq yd), 3 (ft per yd). The only content is 1 sq yd = 9 sq ft. This is a unit-conversion item, which the SAT files under PSDA (ratios, rates, units), not Algebra; the 'linear model' wrapper does not change the construct. No decision point; easy on any route. Not hard by any standard. Drop for difficulty.

SM18L-B2.free_elimination: None strictly free. One addition (14(x+y)=98, x+y=7) makes the key a multiple of 7 and kills 29; 7 and 49 then need x-y=1 or 7. 49 = 7^2 is a closure over the options, not over printed numbers.
SM18L-B2.note: Printed: 9,5,55,5,9,43. Sum/difference gives x+y=7, x-y=3, product 21 - that is the intended insight, but (x,y) = (5,2) are small integers, so a student who just solves the system by elimination is done in three lines. Real SAT versions of this item use non-integer x,y to force the (x+y)(x-y) route; here the insight is a shortcut, not a requirement. 29 = x^2+y^2 is the only distractor with a distinct wrong idea; 7 and 49 are both 'stopped at x+y'. No wrong-method coincidence found for 21 (55-43=12, 55+43=98, neither reaches 21 by one step).

SM18L-B3.free_elimination: None free. A sign argument (target slope positive, so 14-2k and 2k-4 share a sign, so 2<k<7) kills -8 and 17 and even 3 fails only on value - but setting up the slope expression IS the work, so not counted.
SM18L-B3.note: Printed: k,2k,3k,-4,14 (points), 4,-6,7 (line). Roles: 7 is the line's constant and does nothing for slope - a student who uses it is punished, fine. Denominator 2k-4 vanishes at k=2, not offered, fine. Wrong-method coincidence: 7-2 = 5 (constant minus coefficient), weak. Distractors are each a clean slope misread (-2/3, 4, -3/2), which is the best-built distractor set in the batch. Routine algebra reaches the key; no decision point beyond 'parallel means equal slope'. Upper-medium on the real hard route.

SM18L-B4.free_elimination: 420 = 105/0.25 is a quotient of two printed numbers and is struck by a one-division bound: cheaper tiers below 500 mean the average rate is under 0.25, so usage exceeds 105/0.25 = 420.
SM18L-B4.note: Printed: 200,0.12,300,0.18,500,0.25,105. Tier-1 = 24, tier-2 = 54, cost at 500 = 78 < 105, so tier 3; 27/0.25 = 108. Options: 650 stays in tier 2 (would need 115.50 for 650 kWh, so a back-check kills it), 824 skips tier 2. No wrong-method route to 608 found (105-24=81 leads to the distractors, not the key). Multi-step but every step is routine; the only decision is which tier, and the explanation's 'first find the boundaries in dollars' is exactly what the medium route already teaches. Medium.

SM18L-B5.free_elimination: None free. Testing the two endpoints x=12 (19/15>1) and x=-12 (-29/-9>1) shows both rays are live, which kills 4 and 10 as one-sided counts - but that is two evaluations, not free.
SM18L-B5.note: Printed: 2,5,3,1,-12,12. Recounted: (x-8)/(x+3)>0 gives x<-3 or x>8; -12..-4 is 9 integers, 9..12 is 4, total 13. Key correct. But a rational inequality with a denominator case split is NOT an SAT Algebra construct - the SAT never asks students to solve (ax+b)/(cx+d)>1; it is off-blueprint, not merely hard. On the digital test it is also Desmos-bypassable: graph y=(2x-5)/(x+3) and y=1 and count lattice points, or just evaluate 25 integers. Wrong-method coincidence: 25 total integers minus 12 = 13. Hard as pure math, wrong domain.

SM18L-B6.note: Printed: 4,3,18. Recounted by exhaustive scan k in [-2000,2000]: 11 values (k = -27,-12,-7 giving x=3,2,1; k = 4,5,6,8,9,13,18,33 giving x = 34..5). Key correct and the explanation's divisor reasoning is exactly right including the d<-7.5 boundary. But 'for how many integer values of k does a linear equation have a positive-integer solution' is an AMC/number-theory construct - the SAT never counts parameters or asks about divisors of a rewritten numerator. Off-blueprint. Wrong-method coincidence: 18-4-3 = 11, the three printed numbers combine to the key by one subtraction chain; also 8+3 (positive divisors plus the printed 3). Genuinely hard, and unbypassable, in the wrong test.

SM18L-B7.free_elimination: 2 and -2 are both verbatim echoes of the printed coefficient 2 (echo category). Counting the pair as one structural kill.
SM18L-B7.note: Printed: 3,2,16,a,2,6,1,1,7. (x,y) = (2,5); 2a-10 = 6, a = 8. 'Exactly one solution' needs a != -3, not offered, so the clause is decorative. WRONG-METHOD COINCIDENCES, several: 16/2 = 8, 6+2 = 8, 16-6-2 = 8 - three different one-step combinations of printed numbers reach the key. Three concurrent lines with x+y=7 handed over is a standard medium item; here it is easy because the free pair solves in one substitution. Not hard by any route.
